Production of goods with the help of equipment, labor, machines, tools, and chemical or biological processing. Manufacturing is the essence of the secondary sector of the economy. The term covers activity from [[Handicraft|handicraft]] to high technology but is most commonly applied to industrial production, in which raw materials from the primary sector are transformed into finished goods on a large scale. Such goods may be sold to other manufacturers for making more complex products, such as aircraft, household appliances, furniture, sports equipment, or automobiles, or distributed through the tertiary sector to consumers, usually via wholesalers and retailers. Manufacturing engineering designs and optimizes the steps by which raw materials become a final product, beginning with product design and materials specification. Some industries, such as semiconductor and steel manufacturing, use the term fabrication instead.

The English word probably derives from Middle French *manufacture* ("process of making"), from Latin *manū* ("hand") and French *facture* ("making"). Its earliest recorded English use, in the mid-16th century, referred to making products by hand.

Human ancestors made stone tools long before *Homo sapiens* appeared about 200,000 years ago. The earliest method, the Oldowan industry, dates to at least 2.3 million years ago, and the earliest direct evidence of tool use, from Ethiopia, dates to 2.5 million years ago. Stone toolmaking advanced through the prepared-core technique (about 300,000 years ago) and pressure flaking (beginning about 40,000 years ago) to the polished stone tools of the Neolithic. [[Smelting|Smelting]] of copper is believed to have begun when pottery kilns reached sufficiently high temperatures. In the [[Bronze Age]], bronze improved on stone because of its strength and ductility and because it could be cast in molds; the [[Iron Age]] is defined by the widespread making of weapons and tools from iron and steel. Several of the six classic simple machines were invented in [[Mesopotamia]], where the potter's wheel, the first wheel and axle mechanism, appeared in the 5th millennium BC. Egyptian papyrus paper and pottery were mass-produced and exported across the Mediterranean basin.

Papermaking, a 2nd-century Chinese technology, reached the Middle East in the 8th century and Europe through Spain; a paper mill was established in Sicily in the 12th century. The blast furnace came into widespread use in France in the mid 15th century because of cannon casting. The stocking frame, invented in 1598, raised a knitter's output from 100 to 1000 knots per minute.

The [[Industrial Revolution]], from 1760 to the 1830s in Europe and the United States, shifted production from hand methods to machines, with steam and water power, machine tools, and the mechanized factory system. Textiles dominated in employment, output value, and capital invested, with mechanized spinning beginning in Britain in the 1780s. Mass production on [[Assembly line|assembly lines]] was pioneered by [[Henry Ford]] in 1913, followed by automation and digital integration.

Manufacturing accounts for about 15% of world GDP. China produced 32% of global manufacturing value added in 2024 and the United States 15%. Concerns include environmental costs, job losses in high-wage nations, and vulnerable concentrated supply chains, as shown by disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Chinese revolutionary and political theorist, founder of the People's Republic of China (PRC) and its paramount leader from 1949 to 1976. Born to a peasant family in Shaoshan, Hunan, Mao studied in Changsha and was influenced by the [[1911 Revolution]] and by Chinese nationalism and anti-imperialism. He encountered Marxism while working as a librarian at Peking University and in 1921 became a founding member of the [[Chinese Communist Party]] (CCP). He helped build the Chinese Red Army and developed a strategy of guerrilla warfare. In 1935 he became leader of the CCP during the [[Long March]], a retreat to the Yan'an Soviet in Shaanxi. The party allied with the [[Kuomintang]] in 1937, but civil war resumed after Japan's surrender in 1945. Mao defeated the Nationalist government, which withdrew to Taiwan in 1949, and on October 1, 1949, proclaimed the PRC from Tiananmen Square in Beijing.

Most of his political control came through his position as Chairman of the CCP. His government carried out land redistribution and industrialization campaigns, suppressed political opponents, and intervened in the Korean War. A brief liberalization, the Hundred Flowers Campaign, was also suppressed. From 1958 to 1962 he oversaw the [[Great Leap Forward]], which aimed to collectivize agriculture and industrialize the country and was followed by the Great Chinese Famine. In 1966 he launched the [[Cultural Revolution]], marked by violent class struggle, destruction of historical artifacts, and a cult of personality. Mao died in 1976 and was succeeded first by Hua Guofeng, then in 1978 by [[Deng Xiaoping]].

His adaptation of Marxism–Leninism, known as Mao Zedong Thought or [[Maoism]], emphasized protracted people's war and peasant mobilization and has influenced communist movements worldwide.

Assessments differ sharply. Critics describe his rule as a totalitarian regime responsible for tens of millions of deaths, mainly through famine, as well as political persecution, prison labor, and executions. Supporters credit him with ending imperialism, consolidating the Chinese state, and promoting literacy, women's rights, basic healthcare, education, and life expectancy. Under his leadership the PRC replaced the Republic of China as a permanent member of the UN Security Council and became the fifth state to possess nuclear weapons.

Representation or abstraction of geographic reality, the product of [[Cartography|cartography]]. Maps serve navigation, scientific research, governance, and warfare. Route planning is a common use, and specialized maps called charts serve nautical and aviation navigation. Scientists use maps to organize spatial data in geology, meteorology, seismology, and demographics; governments use them for census work, electoral districts, property taxation, dispatching police, and coordinating disaster relief; military and security organizations use them for mission planning, surveillance, border management, logistics, and intelligence analysis.

One of the earliest preserved maps, from the [[Akkadian Empire]] in modern Iraq, is inscribed on a clay tablet and dated to 2300 BCE. By the 5th century BCE, Greeks were drawing maps of their known world. Ptolemy's *Geographia* offered systematic projections in the second century. Maps were important tools in the [[Age of Discovery]], when mariners used them to explore new lands. In the late 17th century thematic maps appeared, portraying data such as rainfall or population density rather than rivers, mountains, and cities. The 20th-century growth of road networks and mass transit created a market for mass-produced maps. Computer cartography and [[Geographic information system|geographic information systems]], developed in the mid-20th century, allowed vast amounts of geographic data to be stored and dynamically displayed; unlike paper maps, interactive maps let users zoom, pan, and choose which data to view.

Designing a map involves selecting and arranging graphical elements so that it is informative, useful, and uncluttered. Because available data often exceeds what can be shown, designers apply generalization to decide what to display and what to omit. Detail depends on map scale, the ratio between a distance on the map and the corresponding ground distance. Every [[Map projection|map projection]] introduces characteristic distortions; the [[Mercator projection]], developed in 1569 for sailing along lines of constant bearing, preserves direction but inflates high-latitude landmasses. Coordinates may be shown as [[Latitude|latitude]] and longitude or on a Cartesian grid, and maps may add legends, scale bars, north arrows, or inset maps.

Definitions of a map have widened over time. The cartographer Erwin Raisz in 1938 defined it as "a conventionalized picture of the Earth's pattern as seen from above, to which lettering is added for identification"; later definitions include digital and tactile media and depictions of things other than the Earth.

Polish-born French physicist and chemist who pioneered research on radioactivity, a term she coined. Born Maria Salomea Skłodowska in [[Warsaw]], then in the Russian Empire, she studied at the clandestine Flying University, which admitted women, and in 1891 followed her elder sister Bronisława to Paris, where she earned her higher degrees. In 1895 she married [[Pierre Curie]], with whom she conducted her early research. She shared the 1903 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics with Pierre and [[Henri Becquerel]] for their joint researches on the radioactivity phenomena Becquerel had discovered. Pierre died in a Paris street accident in 1906, and she became the first woman to hold a professorship at the University of Paris that year.

In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of the elements [[Radium|radium]] and [[Polonium|polonium]], by the isolation of radium and the study of its nature and compounds. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different scientific fields; she and Pierre were the first married couple to win. She named polonium after her native Poland and never lost her sense of Polish identity, teaching her daughters Polish and taking them on visits there.

Under her direction the first studies of treating neoplasms with radioactive isotopes were conducted. She founded the Curie Institute in Paris in 1920 and another in Warsaw in 1932; both remain major medical research centres. During [[World War I]] she developed mobile radiography units, known as *petites Curies*, to provide [[X-ray]] services to field hospitals.

She died in 1934 of aplastic anaemia, likely caused by radiation exposure in her research and radiological work. In 1995 she became the first woman entombed in the Paris Panthéon on her own merits. The synthetic element curium is named in her honour.

Process of acquiring, satisfying, and retaining customers, and a primary component of business management and [[Commerce|commerce]]. Marketing is usually conducted by the seller, typically a [[Retail|retailer]] or manufacturer, and products may be marketed to other businesses (B2B) or directly to consumers (B2C). Tasks are sometimes contracted to marketing, market research, or [[Advertising|advertising]] agencies, and trade associations or government agencies may advertise on behalf of an entire industry or locality.

The American Marketing Association (AMA) currently defines marketing as "the activity, set of institutions, and processes for creating, communicating, delivering, and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, clients, partners, and society at large." The interests of society at large were added in 2008; the AMA's 1935 version described "the performance of business activities that direct the flow of goods, and services from producers to consumers." Philip Kotler defined marketing in 1980 as "satisfying needs and wants through an exchange process" and in 2018 as the process by which companies engage customers, build strong customer relationships, and create customer value in order to capture value in return.

The "marketing concept" holds that an organization should anticipate the needs and wants of potential consumers and satisfy them more effectively than its competitors. It originated in the work of [[Adam Smith]] but did not become widely used until nearly 200 years later. Needs are necessities for a healthy, stable life; wants are desires not essential to survival and often shaped by culture; when backed by ability to pay, both can become economic demands. Market segmentation divides markets into groups of buyers with distinct needs, characteristics, or behaviors. The marketing mix is commonly framed as the four Ps: product, price, place, and promotion.

Historically, marketing shifted from a production focus during the Industrial Revolution to a consumer orientation after World War II. Because it draws on social science, [[Psychology|psychology]], sociology, mathematics, economics, anthropology, and [[Neuroscience|neuroscience]], it is now widely recognized as a science, though it was once seen mainly as a creative industry. One estimate credits marketing investment with 0.18 percentage points of annual U.S. output growth from 1987 to 2020. Critics point to potentially manipulative persuasion, while defenders argue that it facilitates voluntary exchanges that enhance welfare.

Culturally and often legally recognized union between people called spouses, also called matrimony or wedlock. Marriage establishes rights and obligations between spouses, between them and their children, and between them and their in-laws. It is nearly a cultural universal, but its definition varies across cultures, religions, and time. Typically it is an institution in which interpersonal relationships, usually sexual, are acknowledged or sanctioned. A marriage ceremony is called a [[Wedding|wedding]]; a private marriage is sometimes called an elopement. A marriage may be recognized by a state, an organization, a religious authority, a tribal group, a local community, or peers, and is often viewed as a legal [[Contract|contract]].

The word appeared around 1300, borrowed from Old French *mariage* and ultimately from [[Latin]] *maritātus*, "married". The earliest recorded evidence of marriage ceremonies dates to about 2350 BC in [[Mesopotamia]].

Anthropologists have proposed competing definitions. Edvard Westermarck, in 1936, defined marriage as a relation of one or more men to one or more women recognized by custom or law. *Notes and Queries* (1951) defined it by the legitimacy of children born to the woman; Kathleen Gough, studying the polyandrous Nayar of India, accepted legitimacy of offspring as the sole defining element, and Duran Bell criticized that definition as circular. Edmund Leach argued in 1955 that no single definition fits all cultures and listed ten rights marriage may establish, including rights over a spouse's labor and property, a joint fund for the children, and a relationship of affinity between the husband and his wife's brothers.

[[Monogamy|Monogamy]], one spouse at a time or in a lifetime, predominates across cultures, though some societies permit polygyny. Studies link marriage with better health outcomes, but debate continues over whether selection effects or causal benefits explain this. Worldwide trends include equal rights for women within marriage and greater tolerance of interethnic, interfaith, transnational, and same-sex couples, which have gained legal recognition in Western jurisdictions since the late 20th century. Debates persist over dowry and bride price, marriageable age, the legal status of married women, and the criminalization of premarital and extramarital sex. International norms stress free consent and a minimum age.

Fourth planet from the Sun, a desert-like rocky world known as the Red Planet for its orange-red appearance. The color comes from iron oxide on its surface. Its mean diameter is 6,779 km, about half the Earth's, and its surface gravity is roughly a third of Earth's. The tenuous atmosphere is primarily [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]], with surface pressure a few thousandths of Earth's. Temperature ranges from −153 to 20 °C, and cosmic radiation is high. Mars retains some water in the ground and thinly in the atmosphere, forming clouds, fog, frost, permafrost, and polar ice caps with seasonal CO₂ snow, but it has no bodies of liquid surface water. Fine dust is prevalent across the surface and atmosphere.

Terrain follows a north–south divide: the northern hemisphere is mainly flat, low-lying plains, the southern mainly cratered highlands. The planet hosts many enormous extinct volcanoes, the tallest being [[Olympus Mons]] at 21.9 km, and Valles Marineris, one of the largest canyons in the Solar System, 4,000 km long. Marsquakes show that it remains geologically active. Mars has two small, irregularly shaped moons, [[Phobos (moon)|Phobos]] and [[Deimos (moon)|Deimos]]. An [[Axial tilt|axial tilt]] of 25 degrees gives it seasons. A Martian year equals 1.88 Earth years (687 Earth days), and a solar day, or sol, lasts 24.6 hours.

Mars formed about 4.5 billion years ago. During the Noachian period (4.5 to 3.5 billion years ago) its surface was marked by impacts, valley formation, erosion, possible oceans, and the loss of its magnetosphere. The Hesperian period, beginning 3.5 billion years ago, was dominated by volcanism and flooding that carved immense outflow channels. The Amazonian period continues to the present. Because of this history, past or present [[Life on Mars|life]] remains under active scientific investigation, with some possible traces needing further examination.

[[Exploration of Mars|Exploration]] began in 1963 with Mars 1, which lost communication en route. Mariner 4 made the first successful flyby in 1965. In 1971 Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit any body other than the Moon, Sun, or Earth, and Mars 3 made the first successful landing. Probes have been active on Mars continuously since 1997, and more than ten have at times operated at once, more than at any other planet beyond Earth. Crewed missions are often proposed, but none is currently planned.

Codified systems and traditions of combat. They are practiced for self-defense, military and law enforcement training, exercise, ceremony, competition, physical, mental, and spiritual development, entertainment, and the preservation of national cultural heritage. The term originally referred to the traditions of East Asia but has since been applied to practices from elsewhere. It derives from an older [[Latin]] term meaning the "arts of [[Mars (mythology)|Mars]]", the Roman god of war, and was used for European combat systems as early as the 1550s, according to John Clements. Hong Kong martial arts films and performers such as [[Bruce Lee]] popularized it in the 1960s and 1970s. Some authors argue that "fighting arts" is more apt, since many styles were never used or created by professional warriors.

Martial arts may be classified as armed or unarmed, traditional or contemporary, or by intent, such as self-defense, combat sport, demonstration of forms, fitness, or meditation. Unarmed systems focus on strikes (boxing, Muay Thai, karate, taekwondo), on grappling (judo, sumo, aikido, jujutsu), or on both, as in hybrid styles. Armed traditions use bladed weapons and polearms and include eskrima, silat, kalaripayattu, kobudo, kenjutsu, kendo, and historical European martial arts. Korean styles stress spiritual development and "inner peace"; Japanese martial arts are called *budō*, the suffix meaning "way" or "path". Pahlevani and zourkhaneh rituals, the [[UNESCO]] term for a Persian system that once trained warriors, first appeared in its current form in the Safavid era.

Cave paintings from eastern Spain dated between 10,000 and 6,000 BCE show organized groups fighting with bows and arrows, and early Neolithic mass burials in Germany and at Jebel Sahaba in northern Sudan give similar evidence of warfare. [[Wrestling]] is the oldest combat sport; belt wrestling appears in [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamian]] and ancient Egyptian art from c. 3000 BC, and the earliest known depiction of boxing is a Sumerian relief of the 3rd millennium BC. Egyptian tomb art at Beni Hasan, from around 2000 BCE, depicts over 400 distinct wrestling maneuvers.

[[Judo]] and taekwondo achieved Olympic status in the 20th century. Since the 1990s, [[Mixed martial arts]] has combined elements of styles such as Brazilian jiu-jitsu, Muay Thai, and wrestling. Debate continues over traditional forms versus reality-based training tested in unrestricted fights.

German priest, theologian, and author, the seminal figure of the Protestant [[Reformation]]. A former Augustinian friar and professor, he was born in Eisleben and ordained to the priesthood in 1507. He came to reject teachings and practices of the Roman [[Catholic Church]], in particular its view of indulgences and papal authority. In 1517 he wrote the [[Ninety-five Theses]], sent to Archbishop Albert of Mainz; tradition holds that he nailed them to the door of the All Saints' Church in Wittenberg, though modern scholarship considers this unlikely. In 1520 Pope Leo X demanded that he renounce his writings, and when he refused, excommunicated him in January 1521. That year Emperor Charles V condemned him as an outlaw at the Diet of Worms, where he refused to recant. Protected by Frederick the Wise, he translated the New Testament into German at Wartburg Castle.

Luther taught that justification is not earned by human acts or merit but received as the free gift of God's grace through faith in Jesus, and that the [[Bible]] is the only source of divinely revealed knowledge. His beliefs form the basis of [[Lutheranism]], though he himself insisted on the names Christian or Evangelical. His German Bible (1534) made scripture accessible to laypeople, fostered a standard German language, and influenced the English Tyndale Bible. His hymns shaped Protestant congregational singing, and his marriage to the former nun Katharina von Bora set a model for clerical marriage.

Luther's writings also include harsh polemics against Anabaptists, Zwingli, the pope, and Jews. He called for the expulsion of Jews and the burning of synagogues, notably in *On the Jews and Their Lies* (1543), after having argued in 1523 against their mistreatment and for their conversion. He did not advocate murdering Jews, but some historians contend that his rhetoric encouraged antisemitism in [[German language|Germany]] and, centuries later, the [[Nazi Party]]. In 1525 he urged princes to suppress the peasants' uprising. His excommunication was still in effect at his death in 1546.

English writer and philosopher best known for her advocacy of [[Women's rights]]. Born in Spitalfields, London, the second of seven children, she grew up in a family whose income her father gradually squandered on speculative projects. In 1778 she left home to work as a lady's companion, and later set up a school with her sisters and her friend Fanny Blood in Newington Green. She also worked as a governess in Ireland and as a translator and journalist for the radical publisher Joseph Johnson. Her first novel, *Mary: A Fiction* (1788), was partly inspired by Blood's death.

During her brief career she wrote novels, treatises, a travel narrative, a history of the [[French Revolution]], a conduct book, and a children's book. Among her earlier works are *Thoughts on the Education of Daughters* (1787) and *Original Stories from Real Life* (1788). She is best known for [[A Vindication of the Rights of Woman|*A Vindication of the Rights of Woman*]] (1792), which argues that women are not naturally inferior to men but appear so only because they lack education. It proposes that men and women be treated as rational beings and imagines a social order founded on reason. Her support for republican principles and critique of aristocracy emerged amid Enlightenment debates and the revolution, though she stressed moral reform over violent upheaval.

After two ill-fated affairs, with Henry Fuseli and Gilbert Imlay, by whom she had a daughter, Fanny Imlay, she married the philosopher William Godwin. She died at 38, eleven days after giving birth to their daughter Mary, later the author of [[Frankenstein|*Frankenstein*]], leaving several manuscripts unfinished.

Godwin's *Memoir* (1798) revealed her unconventional personal relationships and, though meant as a tribute, damaged her reputation for almost a century. With the rise of the feminist movement around the turn of the 20th century, her advocacy of women's equality and her critique of conventional femininity were increasingly recognized, and she is regarded as one of the founding feminist philosophers.
